item.content:encoded:
We’re down to the final days of the 2026 regular season with still quite a number of teams that have something to play for -- including a few who are fighting for their postseason lives.
Such is the case with the Astros and Rangers, who are tied atop the AL West (with Houston owning the tiebreaker); the team that loses the division will most likely miss the playoffs entirely. Elsewhere in the American League, the Guardians and White Sox are still battling for the division title, though the loser of that should slot into the third wild-card spot.
While all the divisions in the National League have been clinched already, the wild-card race, specifically in terms of seeding, is very much heating up, with the Phillies, Cubs and Padres entering play on Wednesday in a three-way tie.
Which clubs will get to keep playing into October? And which will watch their playoff aspirations come to an end?
Our expert panel has ranked every team based on a combination of what we’ve seen so far and what we already knew going into the 162-game marathon that is a full baseball season. We also asked ESPN MLB experts Bradford Doolittle, Buster Olney and Jorge Castillo to weigh in with an observation for all 30 teams.
1. Milwaukee Brewers
Record: 99-59
Previous ranking: 1
With the season down to a handful of games, the Brewers have all but run out of time for Kyle Harrison to recover his first-half form. Harrison was 8-2 with a 3.01 ERA before the break; he’s 2-3 with a 7.80 ERA since. His strikeout rate has remained steady, even as his velocity and movement measures have become more volatile. Meanwhile, his walk rate has more than doubled, and his homers-allowed rate has nearly tripled. Suffice to say, this is not a great combination of trends. Milwaukee has tried to get Harrison back in stride by using him out of the bullpen, but he’s gotten hammered as a reliever. Brewers fans who dreamed of a big three rotation of Jacob Misiorowski, Harrison and Logan Henderson probably need to recalibrate their expectations at this point. -- Doolittle
2. Los Angeles Dodgers
Record: 97-61
Previous ranking: 2
We’re nearing October baseball, and it’s as if the Dodgers are knocking off items on a to-do list. Shohei Ohtani back in the lineup? Check. Edwin Diaz finding his stuff, finally? Check. Will Smith back in the lineup? Check -- and he has an OPS of close to 1.000 this month. Mookie Betts back to being Mookie Betts? Check. Kyle Tucker digging out of his seasonlong slump? Check. L.A. is putting the pieces back together just in time as it begins its effort to become the first NL team to go back-to-back-to-back. -- Olney
3. Tampa Bay Rays
Record: 96-62
Previous ranking: 3
Tampa Bay began the season with the longest odds to win the AL East. On Tuesday, it clinched its first division title since 2021 with a win over the Yankees. The Rays will enter their first postseason since 2023 as the favorites to win the AL pennant behind a distinct home-field advantage at Tropicana Field, a strong pitching staff and a dynamic lineup centered around MVP candidate Junior Caminero, designated hitter Yandy Diaz and first baseman Jonathan Aranda. With a payroll that ranks 28th in the majors, the Rays seek to become the team with the lowest-ranked payroll to ever win the World Series. -- Castillo
4. Atlanta Braves
Record: 93-65
Previous ranking: 5
Atlanta would’ve preferred to get a first-round bye in the playoffs, of course, but the fact that the Brewers and Dodgers seemed to have locked down the No. 1 and No. 2 seeds allows the Braves to treat this last week of the regular season like the last week of spring training. They can plot out the best way to rest their key relievers, assess the progress of Robert Suarez and arrange at-bats for the position players to be primed for the postseason. Meanwhile, the teams the Braves are likely to face in the first round -- the Phillies, Cubs and Padres -- are all still pushing for berths and home-field advantage in the wild-card round. -- Olney
5. New York Yankees
Record: 91-67
Previous ranking: 4
Despite manager Aaron Boone saying on Tuesday that Aaron Judge isn’t expected to return from his calf strain in time for the wild-card round, Judge told ESPN the following day that he does in fact intend to be ready for Game 1. He suffered the injury last Wednesday and was placed on the injured list two days later. The Yankees were initially cryptic about the setback, declining to disclose the severity and Judge’s outlook.
Boone offered some clarity Tuesday when he called it a “moderate strain” and acknowledged that the club does not plan on having him to open the postseason. Judge received a PPP injection Monday. The Yankees hope that will spur recovery. Otherwise, New York faces an uphill challenge to survive in October without its three-time MVP at his best. -- Castillo
6. Chicago Cubs
Record: 87-71
Previous ranking: 6
No player has made more of a second-half leap than Alex Bregman, whose season has just gathered momentum almost daily since the last week of July. That momentum was stopped in its tracks when Bregman suffered facial fractures last weekend when struck by a foul ball. The good news is that the Cubs decided against placing Bregman on the IL, believing he might be ready for the playoffs after.
But even if that proves to be optimistic, Cubs fans can take solace in the presence of icy-cool rookie Pedro Ramirez. The Cubs didn’t drop off much when Dansby Swanson was injured, as Ramirez provided a league-average bat and glove work at both second and third base that has kept an elite Cubs defense on track. You want Bregman in there, for sure -- but Ramirez provides a heck of a Plan B. -- Doolittle
7. San Diego Padres
Record: 88-70
Previous ranking: 8
San Diego’s magic number for clinching a playoff spot is shrinking, allowing general manager A.J. Preller and skipper Craig Stammen the chance to line up their staff for the wild-card series, with options developing. Stammen indicated to reporters that unless Michael King is needed to clinch a playoff spot on the last day of the regular season, he will be held over to start Game 1 of the wild card, wherever that is -- so he wouldn’t necessarily be used Sunday in order to win home-field advantage in the first round of the playoffs.
Additionally, the Padres are in a better position to rest their bullpen, the perceived strength of the team. Adrian Morejon ranks third among all relievers in innings. Rest might be overrated for Mason Miller: He has made 16 appearances on zero days’ rest, and in those games, he has allowed two hits and one earned run in 16⅔ innings, with two walks and 27 strikeouts. -- Olney
8. Philadelphia Phillies
Record: 87-71
Previous ranking: 7
The culture of Philadelphia’s starting pitchers, from Zack Wheeler to Cristopher Sanchez to Aaron Nola, is to pitch deep into games. Unlike so many starters in this generation, Wheeler takes the mound expecting to work into the late innings -- and the Phillies will need this sort of production from the rotation, given the team’s recent bullpen problems. Orion Kerkering, an important part of the relief corps, struggled so badly that he was sent to the minors last week. Jose Alvarado has pitched better down the stretch, and hard-throwing Alex MacFarlane has quickly ascended into an important role in his rookie season in the bullpen. But the Phillies’ rotation will carry the team’s October dreams. -- Olney
9. Boston Red Sox
Record: 85-73
Previous ranking: 9
The Red Sox rewarded Chad Tracy on Tuesday for leading the team’s historic turnaround by removing his interim tag and giving him a three-year contract to continue as manager. Now he’ll look to accomplish what his predecessor Alex Cora couldn’t last year: beating the Yankees on the road in the AL Wild Card Series.
Boston has cooled off since going 32-5 to put itself in playoff position and faces some injury uncertainty going into October. Ceddanne Rafaela returned Tuesday after missing 16 games with a quad injury, and Willson Contreras was hit by a pitch on his right hand last Thursday and is dealing with soreness. On the mound, the Red Sox could receive two significant reinforcements for the bullpen in Garrett Crochet and Tanner Houck. Crochet, last season’s AL Cy Young runner-up, has been out with a shoulder injury since late April, while Houck hasn’t appeared in a game in 2026. -- Castillo
10. Cleveland Guardians
Record: 82-76
Previous ranking: 12
Cleveland is, once again, showing its knack for a strong finishing kick. Over the past decade, only the Dodgers have won more September games. For Guardians fans aching for their team’s first title since the Truman administration, October is a higher priority at this point.
Like the White Sox, the first order of business is to secure the AL Central title and the first-round bye likely to go with it. Given the neck-and-neck nature of Cleveland’s battle with Chicago, there likely isn’t going to be much time for manager Stephen Vogt to ease up on the pedal to finish the season. That would be nice to do when it comes to rookie ace Parker Messick, who will finish the season with at least 50 more innings than he has ever thrown in a season. Messick has shown no signs of fatigue, so it may not matter. -- Doolittle
11. Arizona Diamondbacks
Record: 84-74
Previous ranking: 10
Manager Torey Lovullo’s comments in a radio interview last week in which he acknowledged that the Diamondbacks “probably” -- his word -- need to reach the postseason to earn him a contract extension surprised many in the industry, as Lovullo has a strong and long-standing relationship with his boss, Mike Hazen. The Ketel Marte situation has been challenging for the organization, with the team’s highest-paid position player failing to show up to the park, and owner Ken Kendrick has a reputation for being mercurial and demanding. Lovullo’s contract runs out at season’s end, and he and the Diamondbacks agreed they would discuss his status then. -- Olney
12. Chicago White Sox
Record: 81-77
Previous ranking: 11
The White Sox have wobbled down the stretch, but they have not fallen down. It looks like they will join the playoff party, completing an incredible two-year turnaround that saw them go from setting the modern single-season loss record to playing in October.
Barring a face-plant over the last few days of the season, the question of whether the Sox can overtake Cleveland for the AL Central title is the biggest remaining question. It’s impactful, with a first-round bye likely on the line. A bye is a boon for any team, but among likely postseason entrants, it might loom largest for the White Sox. That’s just because of how manager Will Venable has had to stretch his pitching resources to the maximum just to get to this point. A wild-card skip would give his staff at least a little time to regroup before the ALDS begins. -- Doolittle
13. Pittsburgh Pirates
Record: 80-78
Previous ranking: 14
Why did Paul Skenes lapse into baseball’s pitching middle class rather than continue his march toward Cooperstown? There is no bigger task for the Pirates and Skenes this offseason than figuring this out. With one more start to go, he has already allowed more runs this season than he did in his first two seasons combined. To be sure, it’s not all on Skenes, whose expected ERA, 3.27 per Statcast, is unusually divergent from his actual ERA (3.91). Still, even a 3.27 ERA is a far cry from the level of effectiveness Skenes flashed before this season. Why? Finding the answer to that question could prove to be the biggest addition Pittsburgh makes this winter. -- Doolittle
14. Texas Rangers
Record: 78-80
Previous ranking: 16
With eyes on the disappointing Mariners and Yordan Alvarez’s Triple Crown watch, the Rangers quietly remained in contention in the historically dreadful AL West all summer. Following three straight losses, they now find themselves tied atop the division with Houston. Texas will host the Mets in a series finale Thursday before finishing the season with three games in Minnesota. The Rangers will need to finish with a better record than the Astros, who own the tiebreaker, to reach the postseason for the first time since winning the 2023 World Series. -- Castillo
15. Houston Astros
Record: 78-80
Previous ranking: 13
The Astros fired general manager Dana Brown last month and are under .500 with four games remaining ... but they still have a real chance to win the division. That’s the AL West in 2026. The Astros finish the regular season with a four-game series in West Sacramento against an A’s team that has an MLB-worst run differential. The bad news: The Astros head there tied atop the division. The good news: They hold the tiebreaker over Texas. In the background over the last few days of the season: Alvarez’s push to become the first player to win a Triple Crown since Miguel Cabrera in 2013. -- Castillo
16. Toronto Blue Jays
Record: 77-82
Previous ranking: 15
The Blue Jays did not replicate their 2025 magic in 2026, largely due to injuries and their offense falling off a cliff. They finished last season fourth in the majors with a 112 wRC+; this season, they’re tied for 24th with a 95 wRC+. The dropoff starts with Vladimir Guerrero Jr. and George Springer. Guerrero has nine home runs -- and, inexplicably, just one at home -- with a .695 OPS in the first year of a 14-year, $500 million contract extension. Springer, who reversed a precipitous decline to hit 32 home runs with a .959 OPS last season, has 15 home runs with a .730 OPS in 124 games this year -- and he’s a free agent after this season. Whether Springer re-signs or not, a rebound in 2027 starts with Guerrero sparking an offense that is tied for last in home runs in 2026. -- Castillo
17. Miami Marlins
Record: 78-80
Previous ranking: 18
Here’s the good news about the Marlins’ 2026 season: They hung around all year, battling among the contenders and having some individual successes. Here’s what’s not-so-great about where they stand right now: It’s hard to identify the players who could lead a Miami breakout into full-scale contention with the best NL teams.
Otto Lopez had an excellent season, but he’ll turn 28 years old next week and his OPS is under .800. Griffin Conine is the one player on the team with an OPS over .800, and he’s 29. Sandy Alcantara reestablished himself as a rotation leader, but he’s 31. Eury Perez has flashes of dominance and is just 23, but he’s got an injury history and will finish this season with an ERA over 4.00. More depth and more talent is needed for the Marlins to take the next step. -- Olney
18. Baltimore Orioles
Record: 78-81
Previous ranking: 19
Another disappointing season in Baltimore has already prompted some changes in the front office, but not at the top. President of baseball operations Mike Elias is expected to return in 2027. One move his front office got right was signing Pete Alonso last winter. The first baseman, who has played in every game this season, hit his 40th home run of the season in Monday’s win over the Blue Jays. He clearly isn’t why the Orioles aren’t going to the postseason for the second straight year.
Baltimore’s young position player core has not lived up to the hype, while the pitching staff wasn’t good enough to shoulder the load. Elias & Co. already decided to move on from former No. 1 pick Adley Rutschman, an All-Star catcher previously considered a foundational player, at the trade deadline. More significant moves could come this offseason. -- Castillo
19. St. Louis Cardinals
Record: 77-81
Previous ranking: 17
This rebuilding season has been an unqualified success for the Cardinals. If not for a leaky bullpen, their soft wild-card contention might have been a lot more solid. While bullpens are sometimes the final piece of the contention puzzle for a building team, that’s not always the case. Some clubs develop a bullpen-building process that takes effect even as the rest of the roster remains a work in progress. The Pirates of recent vintage are a good example.
Thus, the project of putting together a contention-worthy bullpen is a crucial one for the Chaim Bloom-led front office. Bloom was part of a Rays front office that annually churned out elite, no-name bullpens. However, during the four years that Bloom led the Red Sox front office, Boston ranked 24th in bullpen ERA (4.48) and middle-of-the-pack in save percentage. Good first year, but there is more to prove in St. Louis. -- Doolittle
20. Detroit Tigers
Record: 74-85
Previous ranking: 20
The Tigers will probably finish fourth in the AL in run differential, perhaps third if they pass the Red Sox, and will easily pace the Central by that measure. When you consider that, along with Detroit’s freakishly bad record in one- and two-run games (now 21-51) and the relatively short list of players on expiring deals (Jack Flaherty and Gleyber Torres, along with the retiring Justin Verlander), the Tigers are an obvious and very strong bounce-back candidate for the 2027 season. That doesn’t mean that president of baseball operations Scott Harris and his staff don’t have their work cut out for them when it comes to evaluating this lackluster season. Still, for the Tigers’ disappointed fans, it’s important to keep in mind that their team will be proceeding from a relative position of strength. -- Doolittle
21. Washington Nationals
Record: 75-84
Previous ranking: 23
In so many ways, the 2026 season was a success for the Nationals, who exceeded expectations this year, flirting with contention in the first half and seeing the development of players like CJ Abrams and James Wood into offensive stars. But the team’s pitching collapsed in the second half -- Washington’s second-half ERA of 4.49 ranks 25th. The Nationals locked down Cade Cavalli to a multiyear deal last week at the end of what has been a breakout season, but it’s clear that president of baseball operations Paul Toboni’s greatest challenge is to develop the sort of pipeline of pitching that will allow them to compete with the big-market teams in the division. -- Olney
22. Seattle Mariners
Record: 74-84
Previous ranking: 24
A year after falling one win short of the franchise’s first World Series appearance, the Mariners’ season will end Sunday with a whimper. The 2026 campaign will be remembered as the most disappointing one in franchise history.
Cal Raleigh’s drop-off from 60 home runs and an MVP runner-up finish was baffling. Julio Rodriguez regressed and still hasn’t made the superstar jump widely expected of him. Josh Naylor was a below-average hitter in the first year of his five-year contract. The starting rotation was not as good as advertised. Changes are inevitable, likely starting with manager Dan Wilson. But the Mariners can’t fire all of their players. They’ll need their core to bounce back from down seasons in order to rebound in 2027. -- Castillo
23. New York Mets
Record: 73-85
Previous ranking: 21
No one will go into the 2027 season under more pressure than David Stearns, the Mets’ head of baseball operations, following their collapse down the stretch in 2025 and the poor 2026 season. So it makes sense that he worked to keep someone he has a working relationship with in the managerial role, Andy Green, who had his interim tag removed and was hired to a three-year deal Tuesday. Steve Cohen’s comments on an SNY broadcast about needing new voices within the organization got the attention of a lot of rival executives, who wondered if the impact of Pete Alonso’s encore performance at Citi Field and the “Fire Stearns” chants last week made an impression on the owner. Under the circumstances, hiring Green seems like the right move for Stearns, the smart move. -- Olney
24. Minnesota Twins
Record: 75-84
Previous ranking: 22
The arrival of prospects Kaelen Culpepper, Walker Jenkins and Emmanuel Rodriguez has the Twins’ prospective 2027 position group in good shape even if veteran Josh Bell declines his mutual option and departs. The murkiest position is catcher, where Ryan Jeffers is likely headed for free agency, presumably after the Twins issue him a qualifying offer. The QO could limit Jeffers’ market, but probably not that much, as Jeffers looks like the best free agent catcher option out there. If he leaves, the Twins will need someone to pair with Caratini.
Long term, after drafting Vahn Lackey third in the most recent draft, the Twins seem in good shape with him, Eduardo Tait, Khadim Diaw and Carson Tinney all showing well in prospect rankings. Alas, none of that quartet is likely to be a 2027 solution. -- Doolittle
25. Cincinnati Reds
Record: 73-85
Previous ranking: 25
The ongoing maturation of Elly De La Cruz, as he edges toward his career prime, has provided ample reason to keep an eye on the Reds, even amid a last-place showing. Still, there have been enough trade rumors regarding the supremely talented shortstop to make you wonder just how long De La Cruz will be around.
Recent comments made by his agent, Scott Boras, don’t help. Boras suggested to reporters that a future foray into the open market made more sense for De La Cruz than a below-market extension. What does that mean for the Reds in the near term? For now, he has three more years of team control, so there’s no reason to be rash. Still, with this cloud starting to form over Great American Park, some sort of clarity about how the Reds plan to deal with their best player would be nice. -- Doolittle
26. Kansas City Royals
Record: 68-90
Previous ranking: 26
The Royals’ biggest offseason project will be to figure out their 2027 bullpen formula. That process begins with evaluating the relievers already on hand. Presumed closer Carlos Estevez had shoulder surgery -- bafflingly not until the second week of September -- and the Royals almost certainly won’t pick up their 2027 club option on him. Lucas Erceg looked lost before being shipped off to Omaha, but he performed well in Triple-A and his velocity upon his return to the majors has been at its highest level all year. Which Erceg is the real one? Is journeyman righty Nate Pearson a leverage option? Does Craig Kimbrel have anything left? The Royals will need relief help from outside the organization, but how much of it will depend on the outcome of these evaluations and others. -- Doolittle
27. San Francisco Giants
Record: 65-94
Previous ranking: 27
The general perception of San Francisco’s farm system is that it improved in 2026, and Bryce Eldridge established himself as a player the organization could build around. Beyond that, however, the Giants really haven’t progressed. They have a top-heavy payroll situation, with hundreds of millions owed to Rafael Devers, Willy Adames and Matt Chapman. The questions about manager Tony Vitello making the jump from college to professional baseball weren’t quelled by his first season with the Giants -- and neither were the questions about the man who hired him, Buster Posey, who is still relatively new to his front office role. -- Olney
28. Athletics
Record: 63-95
Previous ranking: 28
The A’s are stumbling to the finish line having lost 95 games. All-Star catcher Shea Langeliers recently returned from knee surgery, but several other prominent players remain on the IL, including Nick Kurtz, Tyler Soderstrom, Jacob Wilson, Brent Rooker, Luis Severino and Gage Jump. They’ll enter their season-ending series against the Astros with a negative-217 run differential -- the worst in the majors by 33 runs. With one season remaining before the A’s move to Las Vegas in 2028, they enter the winter in search of a general manager after David Forst’s departure in early August. Their offseason priorities are straightforward: Get healthy and improve a pitching staff that has a 5.43 ERA (29th) despite pitching half its games at the launchpad known as Sutter Health Park. -- Castillo
29. Los Angeles Angels
Record: 60-98
Previous ranking: 29
The Angels, despite 11 straight losing seasons, are the only franchise in the majors that has yet to post a 100-loss season. That could change this weekend in Seattle, where the Angels will need to win three of four games to avoid reaching the century mark. It’d be a fitting conclusion to Arte Moreno’s tenure as owner. Last month, Moreno agreed to sell controlling interest in the team to Stan Kroenke for a record valuation of $4 billion. Kroenke will take over a franchise that has not appeared in the postseason since 2014 and has not won a postseason game since 2009.
The first order of business this offseason will be hiring fired general manager Perry Minasian’s replacement. The team could also be in search of a manager to replace Kurt Suzuki, who is on a one-year contract. It is a transformative time in Anaheim. -- Castillo
30. Colorado Rockies
Record: 57-101
Previous ranking: 30
Colorado has compiled 100 losses for the fourth consecutive season; the last team to suffer 100-plus losses in five consecutive seasons were the Phillies, from 1938 to 1942. In Paul DePodesta’s first year of running Colorado’s baseball operations, there were some under-the-hood improvements: the biggest run differential improvement of all 30 teams in 2026, an improved farm system and some nice finds for the every-day lineup, like Jake McCarthy, TJ Rumfield and Connor Norby. There’s still a long way to go to competitive relevance for the Rockies, especially given the high bar required in the Dodgers’ NL West. -- Olney

Alongside the news that beloved interim skipper Chad Tracy will drop his interim tag, the Boston Red Sox got a slew of positive injury updates. Boston is just six games from the postseason and it needs all the reinforcements it can get.
One of the best, if not the best update is that Willson Contreras is swinging a bat following a scary hit by pitch against the Texas Rangers. Contreras on September 17 took a pitch on the side of his hand, immediately fell to the ground in pain and left the game without delay.
Contreras doesn't easily leave games after being plunked, which has happened 24 times this season. His immediate departure led fans to believe he could've been severely injured. Thankfully, that was not the case, as his imaging came back clean. He believed he fractured his hand because it was numb for a few minutes after the hit, but Contreras avoided the worst.
The Red Sox have not announced an estimated return date for Contreras, but any progress is a good sign. He's been Boston's best hitter all season and leads the team in home runs — the Sox can't afford to go to the postseason without him, especially with the New York Yankees' fearsome rotation ahead in the Wild Card series.
Willson Contreras and Ceddanne Rafaela near returns to Red Sox after both take batting practice on September 22
Ceddanne Rafaela also took batting practice on September 22. He hit off Garrett Crochet, who threw 16 pitches before Contreras' turn in the batter's box. The outfielder on September 19 told Alex Speier of The Boston Globe that he hopes to be active for the final homestand of the season, which has already started.
Like Contreras, Rafaela has been one of Boston's most consistent hitters all year. The Soxs offense has faltered without the two in the lineup. If his timeline holds, Rafaela should be back before the postseason so the Red Sox can take full advantage of his clutch timing in huge moments.
Rumors swirl about Curtis Mead's recovery following Garrett Crochet's BP session
There were also rumors that Curtis Mead was expected to hit off Crochet following Rafaela's practice, but there has been no confirmation that he actually swung a bat. The Red Sox acquired Mead from the Washington Nationals at the trade deadline to bring a righty power bat to their lineup, but he was plunked in his second Red Sox at-bat and the pitch fractured his wrist.
The most recent update on Mead from mid-September was that he was still feeling soreness in his wrist when he tried to swing. The soreness would need to subside for his hitting progression to start, and given the time of the season, many people assumed his year had reached its end. Given that he may not have hit against Crochet, it might still be.
Red Sox send Tanner Houck and Johan Oviedo to Fort Myers to stay loose in case of postseason use
Alongside Crochet, the Red Sox have starters-turned-relievers Tanner Houck and Johan Oviedo nearing the end of their respective recoveries. Both pitchers made rehab assignments with the Triple-A Worcester Red Sox before their season ended and they've been sent to Fort Myers to stay loose just in case Boston needs them in the playoffs, according to Chris Cotillo of MassLive.
The Red Sox will have no shortage of pitching depth entering the playoffs, but whether they use any of their rehabbing pitchers is still yet to be seen. Well-rested arms would be helpful, but the team could be concerned about upsetting the chemistry of the preexisting bullpen, which has been one of the best in the sport all year.

item.content:encoded:
Garrett Crochet reached an important milestone in his road to recovery on Tuesday, facing live hitters on the mound at Fenway Park for the first time since his ill-fated comeback attempt in late May.
Throwing live batting practice against Ceddanne Rafaela, the Red Sox ace threw 16 pitches, one more than originally planned because he spiked a changeup into the dirt on what was supposed to be his final pitch. The left-hander said he was able to ramp up his intensity to a level he hadn’t reached yet, that his fastball was in the 94-96 mph range, and that following the session he got good feedback from Rafaela.
With that crucial box checked, could Crochet’s next time on the mound come in a game setting? Crochet said it’s too soon to say, but he’s cautiously optimistic about his ability to do so.
“You don’t know until you know I suppose. I would say the way that live just went that I could go get outs,” Crochet said. “It depends, obviously, what role they want me in, like I said it’s not really for me to say, I know myself and I know my body, and the biggest thing is that I felt good out there.”
Crochet has missed the majority of the season due to left shoulder inflammation, which landed him on the injured list in late April after only six starts. What was originally believed to be a short-term injury wound up sidelining Crochet for five months and counting, but after Tuesday’s session there remains a possibility Crochet could factor into the postseason equation for the Red Sox out of the bullpen.
That will be up to chief baseball officer Craig Breslow and manager Chad Tracy, Crochet was sure to emphasize.
“This team has had a great year, I think for me to take a spot on the roster then someone would have to lose one, and I would feel bad doing that because this team has pitched their (butts) off the whole season,” Crochet said. “Ultimately that’s going to be something that’s up to the front office and whenever they gauge that I’m ready then I’ll accept that, and in the meantime I’m just going to keep working my butt off.”
Tracy said he was encouraged by Crochet’s outing, noting that his velocity is climbing and the spin on his pitches looked sharp. The next step will be seeing how his body recovers in the upcoming days and mapping out a plan for the weekend.
“What that looks like now, I don’t know,” Tracy said. “I just know that whatever it is it’s going to be done with Garrett’s best interest in mind.”
Typically the next stage in a throwing progression after throwing live batting practice would be to start a rehab assignment, but given that the minor league season ended this past weekend, that isn’t an option for Crochet. Time also isn’t on the left-hander’s side, so if Crochet is going to pitch in a game before the playoffs, he would have to be activated at some point over the final homestand.
Tracy said those are all factors the club is considering, and while he believes Crochet would be up for the challenge of jumping right into a playoff series, they have to be realistic about where he’s at when it comes time to decide who will be on the playoff roster.
“Knowing the player, if he was healthy and we felt he could he’d probably be like ‘I’m not going to be afraid of that,'” Tracy said. “That being said, we have to consider it and just be very mindful of what are we potentially exposing him to and what can he give us, really? Understanding you don’t want to leave yourself short, so for me it’s been step by step, the next step would be sometime this weekend, let’s see what that entails, and we’ll go from there.”
Rafaela, Contreras getting close
Ceddanne Rafaela (right quad strain) and Willson Contreras (bruised right hand) remain sidelined with their respective injuries, but Tracy said both are getting close to a return.
“(Rafaela) is doing much better, we’re getting close there, and Willson’s also doing much better, he was able to swing pretty aggressively in the cage again today,” Tracy said, adding that Rafaela was scheduled to run and Contreras was set to take batting practice on the field. “(We’ll) let them get through their whole day, see where they’re at and assess, but I think we’re getting pretty close with both of them.”
Staying ready
With the minor league season finished the Red Sox have sent a contingent of players who may potentially factor into the club’s plans the rest of the way to Fort Myers so they can stay ready in the event they’re needed.
Tracy did not have the full list of players available when asked Tuesday, but some of those headed to Fort Myers include pitchers Tanner Houck, Johan Oviedo, Jedixson Paez, Tyler Samaniego and Wyatt Olds, infielders Romy Gonzalez, Franklin Arias and Tsung-Che Cheng, and outfielder Braiden Ward.
Veteran catcher Tomas Nido has also come up from Worcester to serve as an extra catcher on the taxi squad for the Red Sox.
Extra innings
The Red Sox announced Eli White underwent successful Lisfranc repair surgery on his right foot Tuesday. The procedure was performed by Dr. Martin O’Malley at the Hospital for Special Surgery in New York City. … Aroldis Chapman (lat tightness) is feeling much better but is still a day or two away from a return to the mound. … Curtis Mead (fractured left wrist) has resumed swinging a regular bat and is taking overhand batting practice, but while the Red Sox haven’t ruled out a possible return, Tracy acknowledged that time isn’t on his side.

Once again, Garrett Crochet donned a full Red Sox uniform, made the walk from the bullpen to the mound, and pitched at Fenway Park on Tuesday afternoon. This time, he faced a live hitter -- in the form of Ceddanne Rafaela -- as he took another step toward returning to the mound for Boston.
And for the first time in what's been a long recovery period, the 27-year-old said he feels ready to contribute.
"I would say, the way that that live [batting practice] just went, that I could go get outs," Crochet told reporters inside the Red Sox clubhouse.
That being said, Crochet shared that he has some hesitance to joining the roster, though it has nothing to do with his own health.
"This team's had a great year. I think that for me to take a spot on the roster, then someone would have to lose one. And I would feel bad doing that, because this team has pitched their ass off the whole season," Crochet said. "Ultimately, that's something that's gonna be up to the front office. And whenever they gauge that I'm ready, then I'll accept that. In the meantime, I'm just gonna keep working my butt off."
More Red Sox Coverage
Crochet's work on Tuesday involved 16 pitches, and he estimated he was sitting at 94-96 mph on his fastball velocity. The left-hander said how well he recovers on Wednesday will be a significant determinant on his ability to pitch in games. Yet when asked if he'll pitch in a regular-season game this weekend or save his return for the postseason, he is leaving that decision to chief baseball officer Craig Breslow and manager Chad Tracy.
"I think that I'm just gonna do whatever they tell me to do, to be honest," he said. "I think that [live BPs] and games, obviously it's a big step up and the pressure of the moment, I suppose, and the intensity. But I don't think that there's a set amount of [live BPs] that need to be thrown before a game."
Tracy, who officially dropped the interim tag earlier in the day, said that whatever decision is made on Crochet, it will be "done with Garrett's best interests in mind."
"Looking at what is he able to accomplish this week, and what does the playoffs require?" Tracy explained. "And then deciding can he fit that role or not based on what he's done."
Ceddanne Rafaela
Rafaela, who hasn't played since Sept. 2 due to a hamstring injury, partook in the live BP with Crochet as he nears a return to the lineup.
"Much better," Tracy said on Rafaela. "Getting close there."
Rafaela has produced the best offensive season of his career, as he's batted .282 with a .760 OPS in 135 games, while continuing to provide Gold Glove-level defense in center field.
Willson Contreras
Tracy also shared a positive injury update on Willson Contreras, who continues to improve after taking a pitch off his right hand last Thursday.
Tracy said that Contreras is "doing much better" and is "swinging aggressively" as he works his way back to full strength.
Aroldis Chapman
Closer Aroldis Chapman hasn't pitched since Sept. 13 due to some lat tightness, but Tracy had yet another positive injury update.
"He's getting very close," Tracy said. "I think we're a day or two away from him being ready to roll."
Group staying ready in Fort Myers
The Red Sox are keeping a team of reinforcements ready in Fort Myers for the playoff run, in case anybody is needed as an injury replacement along the way. That list of players includes:
- SP Tanner Houck
- SP Johan Oviedo
- SS/2B Franklin Arias
- OF Braiden Ward
- RP Wyatt Olds
- SS/2B Tsung-Che Cheng
- RP Tyler Samaniego
- 1B/2B Romy Gonzalez
- RP Jedixson Paez
Curtis Mead
Perhaps the lone negative injury update from Tracy was on second baseman Curtis Mead, who broke his wrist in his first game with the Red Sox on July 27.
"Haven't ruled it out yet. It's gonna be tough," Tracy said when asked if Mead might be able to return for the first round of the playoffs.
Tracy said that Mead is taking some overhand batting practice, but there may not be enough time for Mead to progress to being game-ready.
"I said we would probably be a little aggressive to see how the hand responds," Tracy said. "Have not ruled it out. It's just we're getting up against it a bit."

item.content:encoded:
The Red Sox are officially headed back to the postseason, and by clinching a spot with more than a week to spare, the club now has the luxury of making all of its playoff preparations without stressing about the final six-game homestand.
But there’s still unfinished business to attend to, so here are a few loose threads the Red Sox need to address before Game 1 of the American League Wild Card Series next Tuesday.
Who starts Game 1?
When the Red Sox return to Fenway Park for this week’s penultimate series against the Cleveland Guardians, they will send Payton Tolle, Sonny Gray and Ranger Suarez to the mound, in that order.
Could that be a preview of the AL Wild Card Series rotation? Maybe, but not necessarily.
It’s a testament to the season Tolle has enjoyed that he’s a realistic choice to start Game 1. The rookie left-hander has been fantastic all season, posting a 3.02 ERA over 143 innings through 25 starts, and he’s been especially impressive as the season has gone along.
Gray and Suarez are obviously the more experienced options, but if Tolle is capable of delivering a shutdown playoff performance like Garrett Crochet last fall, there’s merit in sending him out as soon as possible rather than waiting for a do-or-die Game 3 scenario.
If not Tolle, Gray is the obvious choice to start Game 1. Gray has been the ace of the staff ever since Crochet went down in April, and starting the veteran right off the bat would also allow the Red Sox to throw Tolle or Suarez on extra rest no matter which order they chose.
Bello or Bennett as long man?
If there’s a player whose individual season best parallels the 2026 Red Sox, it might be Brayan Bello.
Coming into the year as one of Boston’s longest-tenured starters, Bello completely imploded and lost not just his spot in the Red Sox rotation but his place on the big league roster entirely. But since returning from Triple-A just before the All-Star break, Bello has been fantastic, and last time out he delivered one of the best starts of his career, striking out 11 over eight dominant innings.
Between that and another strong showing against the Angels earlier this month, it appears Bello has finally gotten past whatever issues he was having in the first inning early on. Given that Jake Bennett has been a bit shaky recently, the Red Sox may need to consider the possibility that Bello might actually be the club’s best option as the No. 4 starter should the Red Sox advance to the ALDS.
But there are other factors to consider, too.
With the club only needing three starters for the best-of-three Wild Card series, it would make sense for the Red Sox to leave their No. 4 starter off the wild card roster so they can be lined up and fresh for Game 1 of the ALDS. Since Bennett has never pitched out of the bullpen in his MLB career, and Bello has proven quite adept in that role, it would make sense to stick with Bennett as the No. 4 starter and roster Bello as the long man.
But on the flip side, carrying three starters means the Red Sox won’t need a No. 5 starter either, which means they can add a ninth short-inning reliever on top of the long-man. With all hands on deck and presumably Tolle, Gray and Suarez capable of going deep into the game, the Red Sox could prioritize keeping the preferred Game 1 ALDS starter in reserve, in which case having Bennett as the emergency arm wouldn’t be the end of the world.
Will any rehabbing arms make roster?
With extra spots in the bullpen up for grabs, the Red Sox have to decide if any of their rehabbing arms have progressed to a point where they’re a better option than some of the club’s lower-leverage relievers.
Tanner Houck seems to be the most likely candidate for a bullpen spot at this point. He’s made four appearances out of the bullpen in the minors since the start of September, alternating between 20-pitch short outings and 40-pitch bulk appearances. With the minor league season over and a playoff spot clinched, it wouldn’t be a surprise to see Houck activated this week to pitch in the final homestand, which would both allow the clubs higher leverage arms to stay fresh and potentially serve as a playoff audition for Houck.
How about Crochet? He would almost certainly be limited to one inning at a time, but he also hasn’t faced live hitters yet. If Crochet throws live batting practice this week and comes out looking good, it’s possible the Red Sox could make a bet on his immense upside, though, if the club is serious about not rushing him back it might make sense to hold off until at least the ALDS.
Two longer-shot candidates that can’t be completely ruled out are Johan Oviedo and Kutter Crawford. Oviedo made his first in-game appearance since March last week, throwing 2 1/3 innings for the WooSox in a rehab outing, and Crawford was scheduled to pitch Sunday’s season finale for Worcester before that game was rained out. It would be a surprise if either factors into the playoff picture, but they could conceivably make cameos in Boston this week to help cover some innings down the stretch.
Who will be last man on bench?
The Red Sox are going to have to make some tough decisions when it comes to constructing their bench. Assuming the club carries a back-up catcher — probably Connor Wong — they’ll only have three additional spots and more than a half dozen candidates to fill them.
For starters, which of Isiah Kiner-Falefa, Andruw Monasterio or Romy Gonzalez will serve as the primary back-up right-handed infielder. Would the Red Sox carry two of the three? Or just one to make room for Jahmai Jones as the lefty-killing pinch hitter and emergency outfielder?
How about Mickey Gasper? He’s been one of the club’s best hitters since mid-August and would provide a potent left-handed weapon to use in a late-inning spot against a big righty reliever.
And lastly, do the Red Sox reserve a spot for a dedicated pinch runner like Dave Roberts back in 2004? If so, then maybe Braiden Ward, who just stole 61 bases for the WooSox, might have a chance to make his MLB debut in the playoffs.
Will Mother Nature throw a curveball?
Before the Red Sox even get to the playoffs, they may have to navigate a messy weather situation.
As of this writing, the forecasts indicate a nor’easter could bring heavy rain, gusty winds and coastal flooding to the Boston area throughout the weekend. That is not conducive to playing outdoor baseball, and while the Red Sox probably won’t have anything to play for, the series could have big ramifications for the Chicago Cubs and the National League Wild Card race.
Could the Red Sox wind up having to play a Monday doubleheader to complete the 162-game schedule? MLB will surely do everything it can to avoid that, but the league will be watching the weather closely over the next few days.

Now, they have six regular-season games left to prepare for what is to come.
One big objective will be to get postseason baseball back to Fenway Park for the first time since 2021. After losing in three games in the 2025 AL Wild Card Series to the Yankees at Yankee Stadium, the ending felt too abrupt.
It has already been an improbable turnaround for the Red Sox, surging from 14 games under .500 on June 25 and getting to the postseason. There is a belief within the clubhouse that more magic can happen.
“I think we can make a run,” said rookie lefty Payton Tolle. “I think we’ve got the guys. I think we can get hot. We’re just going to continue to play the way that we play. That team baseball we’ve been playing. You play to get to the postseason and to give yourself a shot to go to the World Series.”
Without further ado, here are some key talking points heading into the playoffs.
What could the postseason roster look like?
C: Adley Rutschman, Connor Wong
1B: Willson Contreras
2B: Nick Sogard
SS: Trevor Story
3B: Caleb Durbin
UTIL: Isiah Kiner-Falefa, Mickey Gasper
OF: Jarren Duran, Ceddanne Rafaela, Wilyer Abreu, Braiden Ward
DH: Roman Anthony, Jahmai Jones
SP: Sonny Gray, Ranger Suarez, Payton Tolle
Bullpen: Aroldis Chapman, Garrett Whitlock, Tyron Guerrero, Erik Miller, Greg Weissert, Brayan Bello, Jake Bennett, Garrett Crochet, Tanner Houck
The most intriguing decision for the position-player roster surrounds whether to add Ward, who set the Triple-A Worcester record with 61 stolen bases this season, as a pinch-running specialist. Dave Roberts, anyone?
The bullpen situation also bears watching. Considering that Crochet hasn’t pitched since April 25 and Houck’s next appearance will be his first in the Majors since 2025, the club will monitor how both rehabbers are throwing before finalizing the roster. This could influence if the club carries Bennett as a reliever. Jovani Morán is another option from the left side.
When does the postseason begin?
For the Red Sox, the fun starts on Sept. 29, when interim manager Chad Tracy’s club participates in an AL Wild Card Series, with all games in the best-of-three series to be played on the road. The Yankees, unless they improbably take the AL East from the Rays, will be the Red Sox opponent in what will be yet another chapter in the richest rivalry in baseball. The only other scenario that can stave off another rivalry match would be the Red Sox slipping to the No. 6 seed. They lead the current No. 6 seed, the White Sox, by four games.
How have the Red Sox performed against the Yankees this season?
Last year, Boston’s hopes of getting a playoff game at Fenway Park for the first time since ‘21 ended when the team lost Game 3 of the Wild Card Series to … the Yankees in the Bronx. So, yes, this would be a rematch between the rivals. In a form befitting the rivalry, the regular-season series swayed back and forth, with New York ultimately taking seven of the 13 head-to-head encounters.
The Yankees swept the Red Sox at Fenway from April 21-23 in what wound up being Alex Cora’s last home series managing Boston. Fast forward to the Bronx from June 5-7, and the sides split, with the middle game getting postponed due to rain. For the Red Sox, their entire season started to turn around with a four-game sweep at Fenway from June 25-28. And for the Yankees, home field for this potential series was essentially wrapped up when they took three out of four from the Sox at the end of August to clinch the season series.
Will Aaron Judge be active for the Wild Card Series?
Judge’s potential participation in the series will be a huge focal point. The Yankees’ captain, limited to 66 games this season, was recently placed on the injured list again with a right calf strain. Though the Yankees have played more games without Judge than with him, his absence could make a difference for Boston.
What happens in the unlikely scenario the Red Sox slip from the No. 5 seed to the No. 6 spot?
In that case, the Red Sox would play the division champion with the worst record, which at this point would be whoever emerges victorious in a shaky AL West.
Which health situations should be monitored as the regular season winds down?
Where to start? There are many to choose from.
Contreras suffered a badly bruised knuckle between his right ring finger and pinkie when he was hit by a pitch on Sept. 17. He admitted he will be out for “days,” but hopes to be back before the postseason. It was a good sign that Contreras was able to grip a bat and take some swings on Sunday.
All eyes will be on Crochet to see if it’s possible to activate him for the playoffs as a reliever even though he hasn’t pitched since April 25 due to left shoulder inflammation.
Rafaela, the Red Sox's All-Star center fielder, has been out since Sept. 3 with a right quadriceps strain but should return before the regular season ends.
How does the rotation line up for the Red Sox?
If not for the near season-long loss of Crochet to this point, the Game 1 starter wouldn’t be in question. Tracy reordered his rotation for the upcoming series, going with Tolle on Tuesday against the Guardians, followed by Gray on Wednesday and Suarez on Thursday. Could this be the same order the Sox open the playoffs with? Tracy isn’t ready to reveal those plans yet.
How much postseason experience does Boston’s projected roster have?
Contreras and Chapman both won World Series rings while playing for the 2016 Cubs. Chapman added another one with the Rangers in ‘23. Kiner-Falefa was with Toronto last season, meaning he got to play in the epic Dodgers-Blue Jays World Series, losing one of the most dramatic Game 7s ever.
Rutschman played in five postseason games during his time with the Orioles, but none beyond the Division Series. Several players in Boston’s young core got their first taste of postseason experience last year in Abreu, Rafaela and Duran. Durbin went to the NLCS with the Brewers in ‘25. Houck and Whitlock are the only players remaining on the Boston team that came two wins from making the World Series in ‘21. Veteran shortstop Story had a solid Wild Card Series in the Bronx last year.
Suarez (4-1, 1.48 ERA in 11 outings, eight starts) had his share of October moments in Philadelphia, and Gray has a 3.26 ERA in six career playoff starts.

item.content:encoded:
The Boston Red Sox are in the playoffs for the second straight year. The clinch became official Sunday when the Braves beat the Astros, guaranteeing Boston a spot in the Wild Card Series starting on September 29.
The roster is not yet complete. Several key arms are still working their way back from injuries, and the next six games at Fenway Park will determine how the pitching staff looks when October arrives.
One of the biggest names on that list took a step forward this week.
Tracy Provides Update on Crochet
Garrett Crochet is closing in on a significant milestone in his comeback. Interim manager Chad Tracy said the plan is for Crochet to throw a live bullpen session against hitters early next week, with Tuesday as the hopeful target.
"Maybe early next week, a potential IBP dependent on how he feels over the next couple days," Tracy said. "Maybe early next week we'll be able to face some hitters. But yeah, tentative."
Crochet's ramp-up has been deliberate at every stage, and the Red Sox are not going to rush the left-hander into a situation he is not ready for.
Facing live hitters would represent the most significant test of Crochet's rehab to this point. He threw 30 pitches over two simulated innings earlier this month, and Tracy said at the time that everything went well. A live session against hitters is the next level up.
What Crochet Would Mean for October
Crochet's potential availability changes the shape of Boston's postseason pitching plans.
The rotation is lining up with Payton Tolle, Sonny Gray, and Ranger Suarez as the likely starters for the Wild Card Series. Tolle has posted a 2.44 ERA across his last eight starts. Gray has been one of the best starters in the American League this season, carrying a 2.76 ERA.
Adding Crochet would give Tracy another weapon to deploy, albeit from the bullpen.
Tyron Guerrero returned from the injured list Sunday and looked sharp. Aroldis Chapman, Garrett Whitlock, and Erik Miller round out a late-inning group that has carried the pitching staff down the stretch. Tanner Houck continues to progress through minor league rehab and remains a potential option.
Final Word for the Red Sox
Garrett Crochet is not back yet. The live bullpen is tentative. The timeline is still dependent on how his body responds day to day.
The Red Sox have been patient with this process, and that patience could pay off at exactly the right time.
Tuesday will tell the story. If Crochet gets through a live session clean, Boston's pitching picture for the postseason gets significantly deeper.

ST. PETERSBURG, Fla. — The Red Sox will start Payton Tolle, Sonny Gray, and Ranger Suarez in the series against the Guardians that starts Tuesday at Fenway Park.
That would conceivably line them up for the Wild Card Series that starts on Sept. 29 with six days rest each.
“Don’t read into that yet,” interim manager Chad Tracy said Sunday before a 5-1 loss against the Rays. “We can line that up still however we want.”
True. But Tolle has a 2.44 ERA in his last eight starts. He also has faced the Yankees twice this season and allowed one run on four hits over 13 innings with three walks and 18 strikeouts.
Gray allowed three runs on nine hits over 13⅔ innings in two starts against the Yankees. He struck out 12 and walked three.
Guerrero returns
Righthanded reliever Tyron Guerrero returned from a 19-day stint on the injured list with shoulder inflammation. Righthanded reliever Wyatt Olds was optioned to Triple-A Worcester.
Guerrero pitched a perfect eighth inning, striking out two.
“Felt good to be out there,” Guerrero said. “If I get a few more games I’ll be fine [for the postseason].”
Guerrero, 35, was called up in May for his first major league stint since 2019. He emerged as a reliable late-inning option, posting a 3.18 ERA over 39 games.
“He’s obviously a very important piece to this puzzle in our bullpen,” Tracy said.
Olds deserved a better fate. The 27-year-old has a 1.20 ERA and 1.20 WHIP in 13 games since making his major league debut on Aug. 17.
“Very tough. He’s thrown the ball great. He’s got big stuff,” Tracy said. “We had to make a roster decision.”
Contreras doing better
Willson Contreras took some swings in the batting cage to test his bruised right hand and came through fine. He said he hopes to be able to do more on Tuesday. “Step in the right direction,” Tracy said … There was no update on Garrett Crochet, who has yet to face hitters. That could come in the next few days … Tanner Houck had a 3.38 ERA over eight innings in four minor league games. Tracy suggested he would face hitters in a simulated game early this week. “Figuring out the next steps at home — and want to figure that out — but no plans for the next outing,” Tracy said. Could Houck be activated? “It’s possible,” Tracy said. “At this point, it’s going to depend very much on where’s the roster at, what are the needs, and then go from there.”… Rays shortstop Taylor Walls showed his baseball acumen in the first inning. With Roman Anthony on first and one out, he allowed Adley Rutschman’s popup to drop. Walls picked up the ball and flipped to second to get the force on Anthony. That left the Sox with a slower runner on first. It ultimately didn’t matter as Trevor Story struck out … Worcester, as Double-A Portland also did last weekend, had its final game rained out. The WooSox finished 76-67. Kutter Crawford was at Polar Park, and the plan was to have him start what would have been a bullpen game. Crawford has not appeared in a major league game since Sept. 28, 2024. He missed the 2025 season because of an injured right knee. He injured his right wrist in August of that season doing yard work at his home in Florida. Crawford pitched three innings in a rehab game for Worcester on April 11 but had a setback and wasn’t cleared for a game until Sunday. “He got to a point where he wanted to go out there and throw one,” Tracy said.

The Boston Red Sox will face off against the Tampa Bay Rays on Sunday in a rubber match on the road and the Red Sox got a reinforcement back just in time for the series finale.
Boston has been missing 2026 breakout flamethrower Tyron Guerrero since Aug. 31. That will change on Sunday afternoon. The Red Sox announced that Guerrero is back and righty Wyatt Olds has been sent down to Triple-A in response.
"The Red Sox today reinstated RHP Tyron Guerrero from the 15-Day Injured List. To make room, Boston optioned RHP Wyatt Olds to Triple-A Worcester," the Red Sox announced.
The Red Sox Got A Key Back
Over the last few weeks, much has been said about the reinforcements coming. Guerrero's return is the first example of this. The 6'8'' righty has a 3.26 ERA and a 36-to-7 strikeout-to-walk ratio in 38 2/3 innings pitched. It had been seven years since Guerrero had pitched in a big league game before the 2026 season. He last pitched in the majors back in 2019 with the Miami Marlins. He's been a breakout story for the Red Sox and now he's back.
Olds has been very good when he has been active on the big league roster this season. He has a 1.20 ERA in 13 appearances this season as a rookie, to go along with a 20-to-7 strikeout-to-walk ratio in 15 innings pitched.
Guerrero is the first reinforcement back for the bullpen, but he isn't likely to be the last. Garrett Crochet and Tanner Houck are two other guys who could be back in the not-so-distant future. Houck is closer than Crochet is. Houck has been on a minor league rehab assignment. Crochet has been tossing bullpens, but hasn't advanced to facing live hitters just yet.
Olds has been good, but it was known that difficult bullpen decisions would be coming. This is the first and we should see more in the coming days.
Guerrero went from unknown among the Red Sox's fanbase, to a high-leverage guy for Boston fairly quickly. Now, he's back as Boston has a chance to clinch a spot in the postseason on Sunday afternoon against the Rays. If the Red Sox take down Tampa Bay, they will officially punch their ticket. Boston's magic number is down to one. A win will get them into the playoffs. Even if they lose, they can make it in on Sunday with losses by other clubs fighting for the Wild Card spots. It could be a big day for Boston and Guerrero's back.

Contreras won’t be on the field for a few days, but he’s still in the clubhouse. That wasn’t the case for Roman Anthony, who was sent to Fort Myers during his rehab, where he worked hard to stay connected to the team. “Just staying in touch with them and seeing what they were doing, I think it’s just the relationship we have,” Anthony said. “As a group, we’re all so close. For me, obviously, Fort Myers wasn’t the most ideal situation, but that’s part of it, and I had a good group of guys down there, and up here.” (Tara Sullivan, Boston Globe)
But now that he’s back in the big leagues, it’s time for Roman to start producing more consistently. He did some extra hitting work before this series against the Rays began and the team is confident he’s going to really get going. “I mean, you see what he can do. It’s the game of baseball, there’s ebbs and flows,” said Chad Tracy. “He came off the rehab, and for like five games, he looked fantastic. Then he went through some stuff, and now he’s starting to look good again. When he’s going well, you see the impact he can make.” (Jen McCaffrey, The Athletic)
Garrett Crochet isn’t with the time right now, but he’s still trying to get back with them. He donned his full uniform yesterday at Polar Park in Worcester and threw 20 pitches, topping out at 92 MPH. The Sox hope he can throw to live hitters at Fenway later this week. Tanner Houck, meanwhile, threw 3.1 innings for the WooSox in his final rehab appearance. (Ian Browne, MLB.com)
A healthy Crochet and Houck could make for a formidable bridge to the back of the bullpen. And after yesterday’s outstanding start, Brayan Bello has also shown that he’s ready to be a part of the postseason action. “For me, it’s just showing the team that I’m ready for these kind of games,” Bello said. “Also, them giving me the opportunity to pitch today was a good step for that. And I thank them for giving me the confidence and the opportunity to start again.” (Rob Bradford, WEEI)
If Crochet and Houck do make it back to the roster, hopefully their transition will be as seamless as Trevor Story’s has been. “The point of getting the surgery was to come back and try to be the player that I know I can be,” he said, “and it’s starting to show.” (Hayden Bird, Boston.com)

item.content:encoded:
The Boston Red Sox are hoping to get one of their key bats back before the calendar flips to October.
Contreras' Injury and Recovery Timeline
Willson Contreras has been dealing with a hand injury after getting hit by a pitch on his right hand earlier in the week in Texas, an injury that's still visibly swollen and bruised days later. According to Peter Abraham of the Boston Globe, Contreras showed reporters the spot on his knuckles where the pitch connected. "When I got hit, I felt my hand going numb. I thought it was bad because that's a sign of a fracture," Contreras said. "That's why I came off the game."
Initial X-rays came back negative, though further imaging is being held off until the swelling subsides. Contreras sounds confident there's no fracture, drawing on past experience with broken bones to gauge the severity this time around.
The first baseman is hoping to take swings as soon as Sunday, though the nature of the injury complicates things given it's on his top hand, the one that absorbs the shock of contact. He's even considered wearing a protective guard over his batting glove if he does return. With Boston off Monday and playing the Rays again Sunday, Tuesday's game against the Guardians looks like the most realistic target for a potential comeback. "I'm going to take it day-to-day. Of course I want to come back and play with the guys and be there for them," Contreras said. "It's a part of baseball."
Contreras has now been hit by a pitch 24 times this season, tied for third-most in the majors, and 47 times across the last two seasons combined. Much of that stems from how close he stands to the plate, and he's voiced frustration about the pattern, at one point suggesting Boston's pitching staff should retaliate on his behalf.
Willson Contreras has more range of motion when he squeezes his hand today than he did yesterday. It remains a day to day monitoring for improvement. He is fairly confident it isn't fractured. He will do everything he can to play through this once symptoms allow.
— Ian Browne (@IanMBrowne) September 19, 2026
Other Red Sox Injury News
Contreras isn't the only Red Sox player working his way back. Center fielder Ceddanne Rafaela has been out since Sept. 3 with a strained right quadriceps. He faced live pitching for the first time since the injury during a Saturday workout in Worcester. "I felt comfortable," Rafaela said. He still needs to test a full-effort sprint before he's cleared. He plans to attempt that Sunday, with a possible return targeted for Tuesday against Cleveland.
On the pitching side, Tanner Houck continued his rehab from elbow surgery. He worked 3.1 innings in a minor league outing that included two strikeouts and no walks. It was his fourth appearance in that process. He could factor into Boston's bullpen plans for the postseason. Left-hander Garrett Crochet hasn't pitched since April 25 due to shoulder inflammation. He's targeting live hitters early this week, likely at Fenway Park. Whether that's enough to earn a postseason roster spot remains unclear. Right-handed reliever Tyron Guerrero could be activated as soon as Sunday after being out since Sept. 1 with a sore shoulder.

item.content:encoded:
Can you believe the playoffs are almost here? A week from today the Red Sox will wrap up their regular season, closing the book on what has been among the most unexpected, topsy turvy seasons we’ve ever seen. From there the playoffs await, and who knows what twists and turns may still be in store.
But before we get there, what business is there left for the Red Sox to get squared away before Game 1 of the Wild Card series? We answer your questions in today’s Red Sox mailbag.
Tanner Houck and Garrett Crochet both appear close to ready to return. What is the chance that the Red Sox decide to put both of them on the postseason roster? Each feels like a high upside question mark but is it too risky relying on both of them to excel in limited roles? — Paul from Bluesky
If the Red Sox decide they’re ready I think there’s a great chance both pitch in the playoffs. The question of whether or not it’s too risky is valid, but the other factor to consider is would it be riskier to let an inferior arm take the mound at Yankee Stadium with the season on the line.
The nature of a best-of-three playoff series compared to a best-of-five or even a best-of-seven also makes the idea of loading up on short-inning relievers more attractive.
The Red Sox will only need three starting pitchers in the first round, presumably Sonny Gray, Ranger Suarez and Payton Tolle, in some order. That effectively frees up two additional bullpen spots, one of which I’m guessing will be filled by Jake Bennett as an emergency bulk man should the starter exit early due to injury or poor performance.
The back end of the bullpen is pretty much set in stone. If everyone is healthy and available it will be Aroldis Chapman, Garrett Whitlock, Erik Miller and Tyron Guerrero locking down the high leverage innings. But after that the Red Sox have some interesting decisions to make.
In one group you have the other short men, including Greg Weissert, Jovani Moran and Wyatt Olds. Then in the next group you have the longer men, including Patrick Sandoval, Brayan Bello, Alec Gamboa and Raymond Burgos. Finally, you have Crochet, Houck and Johan Oviedo, who has also begun a rehab assignment after missing nearly the entire season. What the Red Sox have to decide is which five of those 10 options give you the best chance to win?
I don’t think you can dispute that Crochet and Houck have the highest ceiling of that bunch, so if they’re good to go I don’t think the Red Sox will hesitate to give them the nod.
With Romy Gonzalez now hitting so well in Worcester, do you see him being put on the postseason roster as a lefty masher, and one of Isiah Kiner-Falefa, Andruw Monasterio or Jahmai Jones being left off? — @wcbosox on Bluesky
If the Red Sox believe Romy Gonzalez gives them the best chance to win in October, I feel like it would make sense for them to call him up and get him some looks at big league pitching over the last two weeks. You could make a great case that they should — he was batting .360 in 23 games since being optioned to Triple-A entering Friday — but if that doesn’t happen then that could be a sign the Red Sox don’t see him as part of the October plan.
Either way, the club has some tough decisions to make as far as constructing the bench goes.
Presuming that Ceddanne Rafaela returns from the IL without any issues and Willson Contreras isn’t sidelined by his hand injury, the Red Sox should enter the playoffs with a starting lineup featuring Adley Rutschman at catcher, Contreras, Nick Sogard, Trevor Story and Caleb Durbin across the infield, and an outfield of Rafaela, Wilyer Abreu, Roman Anthony and Jarren Duran, with one of Anthony or Duran presumably starting at designated hitter if a righty is on the mound.
That leaves four spots for Kiner-Falefa, Monasterio, Jones, Mickey Gasper, Connor Wong, Nate Eaton, Gonzalez and possibly Curtis Mead. For our purposes we can probably set aside Eaton, who will likely be optioned upon Rafaela’s activation, as well as Mead, who only just started swinging a light bat and won’t have the benefit of a rehab assignment prior to his return.
Let’s also set aside some of the more outside the box candidates like Braiden Ward, who has never appeared in a big league game but who may garner consideration as a late-inning pinch runner after stealing 60 bases at Triple-A.
One spot will go to a backup catcher, and while you could talk yourself into Gasper filling that role, Wong has the most familiarity with the pitching staff and the Red Sox would probably rather keep Gasper available as a pinch hitter without worrying about catching logistics.
How about the other three spots? Kiner-Falefa, Monasterio and Gonzalez are all versatile infield defenders who bat right-handed, so there’s some redundancy there. Jones also bats right-handed and could function as an emergency reserve outfielder in addition to his pinch hitter, and while Gasper is technically a switch hitter, his real value comes from the left side, where he’s crushed righties over the past month.
What’s going to happen? My guess is the bench will be Wong, Gasper, Jones and one of the three righty infielders. So to go back to your original question, could Gonzalez make the playoff roster over one of Kiner-Falefa, Monasterio or Jones? Yes, and in fact even if he doesn’t make the roster one of those guys could still wind up on the outside looking in.
If the playoffs started today who would be the starting second baseman? Also, what’s the long-term plan for that position? — Tom P.
If the playoffs started today I think Nick Sogard would be the clear choice to start at second base. He’s been an everyday player for the Red Sox since the end of July, and at a time where most of the offense has hit a skid Sogard has been a reliable contributor at the plate, batting .262 with five home runs and a .772 OPS entering the weekend since being called back up on July 29.
Long-term, the Red Sox have a couple of different candidates who could emerge in the coming years.
If he hadn’t broken his wrist in his team debut I think it’s safe to say Curtis Mead would have spent the past two months starting at second for the Red Sox. Prior to the trade he was in the midst of a breakout season with the Washington Nationals, and at only 25 years old there’s good reason to believe his best years are still ahead of him. Whether he returns in the playoffs or for the start of next season, Mead should have the best chance to claim second base for himself.
But outside of him, Sogard and perhaps Gonzalez or Anthony Seigler, there is one other wild card. That’s Franklin Arias.
The top Red Sox prospect is putting the finishing touches on a brilliant season, and if he continues to develop he should have a great chance of becoming a key building block, perhaps as soon as next year. With Story under contract for only one more season he will have an opportunity to slide right into the starting shortstop job entering 2028, but what if he proves he’s ready for primetime before that? In that case Arias might get an initial look at second, with Mead perhaps rotating between the designated hitter spot and occasionally giving Durbin and Contreras a breather at their corner infield positions.
Does MLB need to readjust its postseason schedule? The No. 2 or 3 team in the American League will be eliminated in a three-game series, meanwhile two teams that are barely .500 play each other in the first round. — Brandon C.
I like the idea that there should be a reward for winning your division. If you’re one of the top two division winners you get a first round bye, and if you’re the third division winner you at least get to host the best-of-three Wild Card series. I’m fine with that, even in a weird year like this where all of the American League’s best teams are in the same division and the other division leaders are mediocre at best.
But the problem is what happens afterwards. Like you said, the No. 2 and 3 teams in the AL are probably going to wind up being the Yankees and Red Sox, and whichever of those teams advances will have to play the No. 1 seeded Tampa Bay Rays. Meanwhile, all three teams on the other side of the bracket could potentially finish with worse records than anyone on the AL East side, and one of those clubs will be guaranteed a trip to the ALCS.
I think MLB could address this by reseeding after the Wild Card round. The top two division winners would still get home field advantage in their divisional series, but whichever team advancing out of the Wild Card round has the better record would be paired with the second division winner. So this year if the Red Sox beat the Yankees and let’s say the AL West champion wins their Wild Card series, the Red Sox would go on to play the AL Central champion instead of the Rays, while the AL West champion would get Tampa Bay even though they would have technically started the playoffs as the higher seed.
Most years it probably won’t make a huge difference, but reseeding ahead of the divisional round would strike a balance between preserving the incentives for winning your division while ensuring the bracket doesn’t become unbalanced.

As the Red Sox fell to the Rays 2-1 at Tropicana Field on Saturday evening, wasting an excellent start by homegrown right-hander Brayan Bello, a similar scenario played out between the division rivals’ Triple-A affiliates.
The WooSox lost their penultimate game of the season to the Durham Bulls 4-3 in 10 innings, despite 3 1/3 innings of solid relief work from fellow homegrown Red Sox righty Tanner Houck, who is nearing a return from Tommy John surgery in August 2025.
Houck faced 12 batters, and allowed one earned run and one unearned, on two hits, struck out two and did not issue a walk.
Bulls catcher Tatem Levins scored both runs, but his only true damage off Houck was a one-out 431-foot solo homer in the seventh. Houck’s unearned run came after Sam McWilliams relieved him with one out in the 10th; McWilliams gave up an RBI single to Homer Bush Jr., and Levins scored as the automatic runner.

Houck is the longest-tenured Red Sox major leaguer in the organization, having debuted Sept. 15, 2020. He owns a career 3.97 ERA over six big-league seasons, a mark inflated by his 8.04 ERA in nine starts before the season-ending surgery last year.

ST. PETERSBURG -- While the Red Sox were engaged in a tough battle with the Rays on Saturday, losing 2-1, two of their rehabbing pitchers took steps forward.
Garrett Crochet, the lefty ace who is trying to make it back in time to serve as reliever in the postseason, threw another two-inning side session on Saturday, this one at Polar Park in Worcester, Mass.
If Crochet doesn’t have any ill effects coming out of that session, the Red Sox are hopeful they can have him face hitters at Fenway Park early next week, and perhaps multiple times in the team’s final homestand leading up to the postseason.
“I think it just depends on how he feels coming out of it, how much volume we give him,” said Red Sox interim manager Chad Tracy. “So it's hard to say. I know it's not a great answer, but it's just really how it is. How does he feel after each step? So when he does that, how does he feel? And then determine from there. Do we give him more hitters or do we want to put him in a game? It’s hard to say until you know how he feels.”
Meanwhile, righty Tanner Houck made his final rehab appearance for Triple-A Worcester, allowing two hits and two runs (one earned) over 3 1/3 innings. Houck walked none and struck out two as he continued to make progress in his return from Tommy John surgery.
As is the case with Crochet, Houck doesn’t have time to build back up as a starter, but he could be a bullpen option for the Sox in October.
Perhaps Houck could make an appearance or two during the season-ending homestand against the Guardians and Cubs, which starts Tuesday.
